How We Think: A Theory of Goal-Oriented Decision Making and Its Educational Applications
Teachers make instructional moves and students reply; students initiate some action and teachers respond
Experienced educators under- stand that there is a rhythm, a tempo, evident in all that instructional chaos
However, it is not arhythm that can often be precisely or reliably reproduced, or even readily anticipated

Certainly there are routines or subroutines, what Schoenfeld and others refer to as scripts or schemas (Anderson, Reynolds, Schallert, & Goetz, 1977; Mandler, 1984; Mason & Morris, 2010), thatcan be recognized and named
For instance, there is the prologue, where teachers introduce the lesson to follow and students acknowledge their expected role in that lesson
There is the review or wrap-up, when students are called on to communicate what they have already learned or canperform or the teacher reiterates what was “learned” in the preceding activities

But overall, the ﬂow of the entire lesson cycle far overruns these particular recognizable instructional episodes and far outreaches one’s abilities to predict what teachers will do next or why such action will betaken

THE GENERAL STRUCTURE OF HOW WE THINK As Schoenfeld seeks to establish in his volume, How We Think: A Theory of Goal-Oriented Decision Making and its Educational Applications , there is more predictability than meets the eye in the instructional ﬂow of the classroom

His contention is that if we, as perceptive observers, enter the classroom chaos armed with critical information about a speciﬁc teacher, then theinstructional movements that teacher makes and the choices those movements expose become more predictable and more understandable—less chaotic in appearance

Speciﬁcally, building on decades of his empirical work on problem solving, especially in the domain of mathematics,Schoenfeld sets out to make a strong case that teachers’ instructional decision making—a form of problem solving—is a function of the goals they set for the instruction, the resources upon Downloaded by [Erciyes University] at 21:46 28 December 2014

The instructional goals or purposes can be conscious and intended or they may be more tacit in form
The resources to which Schoenfeld refers encompass primarily the teachers’ knowl- edge about the domain, task, and pedagogy
Moreover, the orientations component he identiﬁesencompasses what teachers hold to be true about the domain, teaching, and the learner

To use Schoenfeld’s own words, the claim “at the heart” of this book is the following: If you can understand (a) the teacher’s agenda and the routine ways in which the teacher tries to meet the goals that are implicit or explicit in that agenda, and (b) the factors that shape the teacher’s prioritizing and goal setting when potentially consequential unforeseen events arise, then you can explain how and why teachers make the moment-by-moment choices they make as they teach
10) Throughout the chapters of How We Think , Schoenfeld delves into each of these key areas
He thoughtfully explains each (Chapters 1–3) and describes how they form the bases of his the- ory of goal-oriented decision making

Next, he illustrates the inﬂuence of goals, resources, andorientations as well as the ecological validity of his theoretical model through detailed analyses of transcripts of mathematics and science lessons (Chapters 4–6)
For instance, in Chapter 6, he meticulously walks us through a segment of a lesson in a third-grade classroom dealing withthe properties of even and odd numbers
The lesson he analyzes was taught by Deborah Ball, a renowned mathematics educator and researcher

He uses the transcripts from this lesson segment to illustrate how what he initially judged as surprising pedagogical movements by Ball becameincreasingly clearer once he began to take into account her goals, resources, and her espoused orientations
In the closing chapters of the volume (Chapters 7 and 8), Schoenfeld moves away from the territories of mathematics and science and ventures into the ﬁeld of medical consultation
His intentions appear to demonstrate the broad applicability of his theory to domains that appear appreciably different from mathematics or science education
He also wanted to consider jointproblem solving that arises between doctor and patient during the consultation process

The intriguing feature of this extension and generalization is that Schoenfeld delves into a personal medical issue, adult onset (Type II) diabetes, and his interactions with a doctor with whom he is very familiar
Does he craft a convincing and com- pelling argument for his theory of goal-oriented decision making

To answer that question, I want to loosely apply Schoenfeld’s three key dimensions, goals, resources, and orientations, not to ascertain whether I understand what he did or why—since he thoughtfully details all of thatfor the reader—but rather to judge whether his goals and associated decisions worked for me as a reader of this volume

Speciﬁcally, I ask how effectively Schoenfeld’s goals and orienta- tion are manifest within the pages of this volume; whether the treatment of resources, especiallywith regard to domain and pedagogical knowledge, is sufﬁciently represented; and how well the process of decision-making is explicated and justiﬁed

If I were to characterize the orientation represented within the pages of How We Think , I would have to borrow a term I have used to signify my own orientation to learning, cognitive Downloaded by [Erciyes University] at 21:46 28 December 2014

BOOK REVIEW 259 contextualism (Alexander, Schallert, & Reynolds, 2009); an orientation that appreciates the thinking and reasoning of the individual mind while duly acknowledging the power of the social collective and contextual factors

One of the evident strengths of this book is its ability to speak to the diverse community of mathematics and science education as a consequence ofthis multidimensional orientation to human learning and performance

For instance, the metic- ulous moment-by-moment analysis of skilled teachers’ pedagogical movements in light of their goals, orientation, and knowledge is evidence of Schoenfeld’s extensive understanding of humancognition and his roots in both mathematics and cognitive science
Few could have brought the requisite analytic structure and perspective to these mathematics and physics lessons
It is also apparent that Schoenfeld’s orientation toward decision making is not restricted to the mental ruminations of a teacher operating in a sociocontextual vacuum
Each step in the decision- making chain is shaped by the actions of others and by the co-constructed understandings thatarise
Clearly, his theory of goal-oriented decision making would not be meaningful without this sociocontextual dynamic
Of course, orientation, for Schoenfeld, is not solely a matter of one’s beliefs about the nature of learning in general, but also about mathematics or science and how those subjects should be taught

For instance, considering a lesson segment on blood alcohol content, Schoenfeld encap-sulates the orientation of Jim Minstrell, a recipient of the Presidential Award for Excellence in Mathematics and Science Teaching, thus: Minstrell conceives of physics (and thus of physics learning) as a sense-making activity, and he believes that students’ classroom experiences should support the development of their abilities as sense makers ...
Minstrell believes that his students need to engage directly with the material and not simply be told what works
Hence Minstrell works to create a discourse community thatinvolves small-group work among students, and he structures teacher-student exchanges in a way that minimizes “telling.” (pp

90–91) Overall, I ﬁnd that Schoenfeld’s perspective and the evidence that he offers in its support work best when the potential audience is educational researchers interested in identifying thepatterns within teachers’ instructional actions
I am not convinced of the practical utility of this theoretical model for practicing teachers seeking to understand their own decision making or that of their peers

Decisions within the classroom are simply too numerous and multifacetedin their nature, and progress at such a rate and tempo that only a few lesson segments could be systematically dissected in such a pedagogical postmortem as we ﬁnd in these chapters

Likewise, while I applaud Schoenfeld’s attempt to move the theory away from mathematics and physicsteaching and beyond the conﬁnes of the classroom, and even though the interactions between doctor and patient are both thoughtfully and sensibly analyzed, I see this effort to generalize the model as less convincing or compelling
The book and the theoretical model are at theirbest when the focus remains squarely on the thinking and reasoning of mathematics or science teachers during the course of instructional decision making
The aforementioned criticisms are not meant to cast doubts on the contributions of this theo- retical work in general or this volume in particular

Mathematical researchers can beneﬁt greatly from understanding the parameters of Schoenfeld’s theory and the relations his theoretical model hypothesizes, as well as from the data-analytic system he has applied in capturing classroom inter-actions

Two aspects of Schoenfeld’s presentation of resources in How We Think merit discussion here

First, while Schoenfeld uses the more general word, resources, to characterize a signiﬁcant aspect of goal-directed decision making, the discussion throughout the book and in the researchupon which this book is based deals almost exclusively with knowledge

Given Schoenfeld’s impressive body of work on mathematical problem solving within the educational psychological literature, it was not surprising to see domain and pedagogical knowledge so prominently dis- played within the resource dimension of his goal-oriented decision-making theory
Further, it is hard to take issue with any of the knowledge principles outlined in the introduction of this volumeand that frame subsequent analyses in the ensuing chapters
Insights into the knowledge base of teachers can go a long way to explain what they perceive within the ﬂow of instruction and to what they allocate their attention
The discussion of Mark Nelson’s Algebra I lesson in Chapter 4 solidly positions the inﬂuence of teacher domain and pedagogical knowledge in decision making
In this chapter, Schoenfeld expertly deconstructs this student teacher’s hour-long session on dividing expressions withexponents and makes the following observations regarding Nelson’s resources
The arithmetic of exponents was familiar territory for Nelson, who was well prepared mathematically

The pedagogical resource he relied on in give-and-take sessions with students was a questioning strategy in which he asked students for the answers to problems he had given them and then provided feedback on their responses ...
Finally, given that this was the ﬁrst time teaching this particular material, Nelson could not be expected to have a reservoir of pedagogical content knowledge for this topic ...
Such knowledge is developed with experience, if it is developed at all
77) A second aspect that warrants discussion pertains to the orientation toward knowledge that the goal-oriented decision-making theory represents
One of the clear strengths of this book is the treatment of content and pedagogical knowledge at the declarative, conceptual, and procedurallevels

With each detailed analysis, Schoenfeld provides persuasive evidence of how expertise and its associated knowledge come into play in the decision making of the teachers—Nelson, Minstrell, and Ball—and Dr.B
The relations between expertise and decision making havebeen well documented by others within the educational literature (Alexander, 2003; Ericsson, Charness, Feltovich, & Hoffman, 2006)
But, few have illustrated that relation with the precision and care found in the pages of this book

That being said, although Schoenfeld’s treatment of orientation within the chapters of this book pays homage to individuals’ beliefs about the nature of their domains, there is much theo- retical and empirical work on epistemology or epistemic beliefs that could add to this dimensionof the overall theoretical model

What is essential to keep in mind is that the theoretical model Schoenfeld proffers pertains to goal-oriented decision making in well-practiced, knowledge-intensive domains

What cannot be explicated by this theory or by any other cognitive or sociocognitive model are the sponta- neous choices that individuals repeatedly make whether in classrooms, in doctor’s ofﬁces, or with any tasks that are not highly proceduralized or routinized
Many human actions, including decisions, do not arise from conscious or rational thought
If there is rationalization involved insuch choices, it may come in the form of post hoc justiﬁcations or explanations
Goal-oriented decision making rests on the assumption that decisions on the part of the teacher are the result of a deliberate and conscious process

Some portion of those goal-directed decisions fall in theclass that Schoenfeld classiﬁes as routine decision making, “relatively unproblematic” forms of decision making that are instantiations of well-practiced scripts and schemes
The challenge, as Schoenfeld rightly notes, is when the routine scripts or schemes cannot be fully enacted, as whennonroutine situations are encountered

Through all the step-by-step analyses of transcripts from beginning or master teachers engaged in mathematics or physics instruction or from an established physician involved in doctor-patientconsultation, accompanied by numerous graphics and ﬂow charts, Schoenfeld methodically builds his case for his theory

Interestingly, as with others in the educational community seek- ing to problematize mathematics and science instruction, Schoenfeld is determined to reduce thenoise within classroom data—to ﬁnd a workable path through the labyrinth
TAKING STOCK, APPLICATIONS, AND NEXT STEPS Taking Stock So the lingering question remains whether the goals Schoenfeld set for himself and for this vol- ume were achieved
Am I persuaded by the detailed cases he offers and is his proof compelling and irrefutable

And most importantly for this review, do I regard this compilation and extension of Schoenfeld’syears of research to be a work that belongs in the library of educators concerned with teaching and learning

I concur with Schoenfeld when he states that, “theories and models in science are always subject to revision and reﬁnement,” that they must be built on “certain assumptions about the nature of mental organization,” (p
